title: [API] Add ModelWarmup image preloading
body:
## Pull Request Description

Adds the namespaced `model.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1` `ModelWarmup` API for preloading container images onto explicitly selected Kubernetes nodes.

- supports explicit node names and label selectors with union/deduplication and source reporting
- creates safe, node-pinned Jobs with configurable image pull policy, parallelism, timeout, retries, TTL, and pull secrets
- reports per-node diagnostics, aggregate status, mutually exclusive Ready/Progressing/Degraded conditions, and deterministic revisions
- adds mutating/defaulting and validating admission webhooks
- includes generated clients/CRD/RBAC/webhook manifests, samples, and user documentation
- adds unit, controller/webhook integration, and live-cluster E2E coverage for success, selector expansion, image cache reuse, admission, and failure paths

title: [Feat] Map the request SLO tier to the vLLM request priority
body:
### Pull Request Description

Requests that share a model endpoint have different latency needs, and there is currently no way for a caller to say which one it is. An interactive turn can end up queued behind a nightly batch backfill even though the batch job would be perfectly happy to wait.

This adds the opt-in mapping proposed in #2286, with the v0 scope that was stated there. When `AIBRIX_SLO_TIER_PRIORITY_ENABLED=true`, a request carrying the `x-aibrix-slo-tier` header has the matching value written into the `priority` field of its backend request body:

| `x-aibrix-slo-tier` | `priority` | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `batch` | `100` | Below the engine default of `0`, so batch work yields to interactive requests. |
| `background` | `1000` | Yields to both interactive and `batch` work. |
| _(other or missing)_ | _(unchanged)_ | Forwarded untouched. |

vLLM serves smaller `priority` values first, so both entries sit below the engine default of `0` and the mapping can only de-prioritize. There is no path by which enabling this feature pulls a request ahead of one that did not set a tier, which is what makes it safe to switch on for a shared endpoint. The engine does the actual scheduling, so vLLM deployments need a priority-aware scheduler (`--scheduling-policy=priority`) for the field to have an effect.

### Semantics

- **Off by default.** While `AIBRIX_SLO_TIER_PRIORITY_ENABLED` is unset or `false`, the header is ignored and request bodies are forwarded byte for byte. There is no behavior change for existing deployments.
- **De-prioritize only.** The table has no value that outranks a request without a tier. A latency-sensitive tier can get an explicit head start later if that is wanted; doing it in a separate change keeps this one incapable of delaying traffic that opted out of nothing.
- **The caller wins.** A `priority` already present in the request body is never overwritten, so a client can pick a value for a tier the table maps, or use the field directly for a tier it does not.
- **Fail-open.** A body sjson cannot extend (not a JSON object, truncated, or a non-JSON endpoint such as the multipart audio and video paths) is forwarded unchanged. The tier is a hint and never fails or blocks a request.
- **No new artifact.** The tier rides on a request header rather than a new CRD or profile field, which keeps this usable from any client the gateway already serves.
- Tier names are matched case-insensitively and survive surrounding whitespace.

### Implementation

- `pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway_req_priority.go` holds the tier table and the rewrite. The body is edited with `sjson`, the same helper the PD path uses, so no field other than `priority` changes.
- `gateway_req_headers.go` records the header on the routing context.
- `gateway_req_body.go` applies the mapping once a target is chosen, so the rewrite lands on the same bytes the request forwards, and the `content-length` sent to Envoy is recomputed from it. Both the routed and the `RouterNotSet` paths go through the same call. The `RouterNotSet` path gains that header because a body rewrite changes its size, and the size is what Envoy validates the upstream request against; while the opt-in is off the body is untouched and the header the handler sets matches the length that would have been sent anyway.
- `cmd/plugins/main.go` reads the new environment variable, defaulting to `false`.

### Test Plan

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...`, `staticcheck -checks='QF*'`, and a `sphinx-build -W --keep-going` pass are all clean.
- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/types/... ./cmd/...` passes.
- New tests in `gateway_req_priority_test.go` cover the tier lookup (case-insensitive, unknown, empty, whitespace-only), the injection rules on the routing context alone (opt-out byte-for-byte, unmapped tier, caller-set `priority` including `0`, non-object body), and the end-to-end handler in both dispatch modes: routed and unrouted, with and without a mapped tier, each asserting the `content-length` header matches the forwarded body. Removing the `RouterNotSet` content-length line makes the two unrouted cases fail, so that part of the change is pinned rather than incidental.
- `gateway_req_body_test.go` asserts the exact header set of an unrouted request, now including `content-length: 74` for a 74-byte body, which is what pins the opt-out path as byte-for-byte.

### Notes

- `docs/source/features/gateway-plugins.rst` and `pkg/plugins/gateway/ENV_VARS.md` are also touched by #2786. The additions here are placed away from that change's hunks (a new section before **Headers Reference** and one table row at the end of **Target and General Headers**), so the two should merge cleanly in either order, but the overlap is worth knowing about.

Refs #2286

title: [Feat] Drive gateway routing thresholds from model config profiles
body:
## Pull Request Description

#1961 asks for the gateway plugin configuration to move onto routing profiles, split into what needs backward compatibility and what does not. This PR moves the per-request routing thresholds a model config profile (`model.aibrix.ai/config`) can select for its own requests into `routingConfig` (plus the model-level `ttftThresholdS`), with the environment as the fallback default: a deployment without these fields routes exactly as before.

**What moves into the profile**

- `ttftThresholdS` (top level, next to `routingStrategy`): overrides `AIBRIX_TTFT_THRESHOLD_S` for the profile's first-token-delay classification.
- `routingConfig.pd.*`: the decode abort timeout and retry delay, the four imbalance spread thresholds, the decode load-balance weights, the token-load charge knobs, `hybridCacheLoadFactor`, `minMatchPct` and `prefillRequestTimeout`.
- `routingConfig.promptLengthBucketing` (flat, next to `promptLenBucket*`), `routingConfig.loadBalance.*`, `routingConfig.prefixCache.standardDeviationFactor`, `routingConfig.preble.targetGPU` and `decodingLength`, `routingConfig.vtc.*`, and `routingConfig.autoBlend.*`.

**Compatibility and semantics**

- Every knob keeps its matching `AIBRIX_*` variable as the default. A knob the profile leaves unset, or sets to a value the variable would reject (a negative factor, a percentage outside its range, an unknown GPU name), is dropped at the profile boundary, so a profile can only narrow or sharpen routing behavior and a deployment without these fields routes exactly as before.
- Knobs that configure process-wide state stay environment-only on purpose, because all models of one gateway process share that state: the preble histogram window and eviction loop, the VTC token tracker window, time unit and token floors plus its input/output token weights, the session-affinity local cache capacity, and the router string cache bound. The docs list them explicitly.
- Deployment-level settings (tokenizer endpoints, Redis and statesync settings, the rate limiting switches, `AIBRIX_KV_CONNECTOR_TYPE`) also stay environment-only, as before.
- The knobs are resolved once per request. The non-PD path parks them on the `RoutingContext`, and `reset` clears them so a pooled context cannot leak the previous request's thresholds into a request whose profile sets none. The PD path parks them on the `PDLegState`, because the async prefill goroutine and the decode abort outlive the client stream and must not read a recycled routing context.

**Docs**

`gateway-plugins.rst` gains a per-request routing knobs table (field, overridden variable, description) and the environment-only list; `ENV_VARS.md` gains a variable-to-field mapping section; the PD and model-deployment pages point at the new section.

## Test Plan

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./pkg/types/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...`, `gofmt` clean.
- `go test ./pkg/types/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... -count=1`: the new tests cover the environment default without a profile, the profile value reaching every scoring, charge and filter site when set, invalid values keeping the environment default, and `RoutingContext.reset` clearing the knobs.
- `sphinx-build -b html -W --keep-going docs/source docs/_build/html` clean for the docs changes.

## Related Issues

Refs #1961

title: [Feat] Route vLLM /pooling requests through the gateway
body:
## Pull Request Description vLLM serves pooling models (embed/classify/score tasks) at a native /pooling endpoint, but the gateway's hardcoded path switch in validateRequestBody had no case for it, so pooling requests were rejected with 404 "not found" before ever reaching an engine. Users deploying embedding or scoring models behind AIBrix could only reach them through the OpenAI-shaped /v1/embeddings, which does not exist for classify/score tasks and cannot express vLLM's pre-tokenized input form. Add PathPooling plus a validator that requires only "model" -- the one field the gateway routes on -- and forwards the body verbatim; the engine owns the rest of the schema validation. Input is held as raw JSON rather than a typed field because vLLM accepts a string, an array of strings, or a pre-tokenized array of token ids, and a wrongly-typed input must reach the engine's validator, which names the offending field, instead of collapsing into a generic gateway 400. A body with no input at all still reaches the engine, which owns that error too. Stream is rejected when present and true, as for embeddings: pooling never streams, and a stream=true body would otherwise be forwarded just to fail in the engine with a less specific error. Verified with gofmt, golangci-lint, go vet, and go test on ./pkg/plugins/gateway/ and ./pkg/controller/modelrouter/ (including the generated-xDS consistency test), all passing. ## Related Issues Resolves: #[Insert issue number(s)] **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [CI] Cancel superseded pull-request workflow runs
body:
## Pull Request Description

Superseded runs stay in the queue and keep holding runners while the newest push waits behind them.

Measured on 2026-09-22 (UTC) in this repository:

- At 07:39Z, 31 workflow runs were queued or in progress, and 12 of them were already at a commit that is no longer the head of its pull request. One of those had been waiting since 03:17Z.
- Queue time dominates the wall clock. Sampled `Linter and Unit Tests` runs waited 38 minutes to 2 hours 35 minutes for their first job, while the jobs themselves run in 2 to 9 minutes.
- A pull request pushed at 06:56Z had 19 checks. Its first job started 30 minutes later, and the remaining checks were still queued 45 minutes after the push.

Changes:

- Add a `concurrency` group to the workflows that run on pull requests. The group is keyed on the pull request number, so a newer push cancels the run it supersedes. `push` and `workflow_dispatch` runs fall back to a per-run group, so their behavior is unchanged. The triage bot uses the issue or pull request number.
- Add `timeout-minutes` to jobs that did not set one. The default is 360 minutes, so a job that hangs can hold a runner for six hours. The values stay well above the observed runtimes. The longest job, `Installation E2E Tests`, already takes about 41 minutes and is capped at 75.

Nothing changes about what is verified: the checks that gate a pull request always run for its current head. Cancel-in-progress only drops runs for commits that a newer push has already replaced.

## Related Issues
N/A

## Test Plan
- `actionlint` on all workflow files: no new findings (the six pre-existing shellcheck notices in `lint-and-tests.yml` and `installation-tests.yml` are unchanged).
- All workflow files parse as YAML, and every job in the touched workflows now carries a timeout.
- `timeout-minutes` values were compared against job durations from recent runs (`Installation E2E Tests` 2422 to 2472 seconds, `Go Race Tests` about 9 minutes, smoke image builds 1 to 6 minutes).
- `git diff --check` clean.

title: [Bug] Include canonicalized tools in the prefix-match text
body:
## Pull Request Description The routing message the gateway uses for prefix matching is built from `messages[].content` only. Many chat templates render the tool definitions ahead of the conversation, so two requests with the same messages but different `tools` differ in the engine prompt from the first tokens. The gateway nevertheless treats them as a 100% prefix match and pins them to the same pod. This PR prepends a canonical rendering of `tools` to the routing message of `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` requests, separated by a single space: - The rendering sorts object keys at every level, is compact, does not escape HTML characters and keeps number literals as sent, so the same tools produce the same text whatever the client's key order or whitespace. - Absent, `null` or empty `tools` leave the routing message byte-identical to today. - `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_INCLUDE_TOOLS` (default `true`, read once at startup) restores the messages-only behavior when set to `false`. - The change sits in `parseChatMessages`, the function `validateChatRequest` uses to build the routing message. `/v1/responses`, `/tokenize` and `/v1/completions` pass no tools and are unchanged. Templates differ in where they place tools: most render them in the system block ahead of the conversation, which this ordering matches; a few (e.g. Mistral) place them near the last user turn. For those templates the routing text is less accurate: requests that share tools but not messages can see a partial match the engine won't have. Such deployments can set `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_INCLUDE_TOOLS=false`. **Affected policies:** `prefix-cache`, `prefix-cache-preble`, and the PD prefill policies `prefix_cache`, `conductor` and `hybrid_cache_load`. In KV-sync mode with a remote tokenizer, the chat-template path still tokenizes the messages only, so tools apply there only on the plain-text fallback. **Side effect, documented in ENV_VARS.md:** the routing message also drives several prompt-size estimates, which now count the tools as well: - VTC token estimates - `RoutingContext.PromptTokens` / `PromptLength`, used by the SLO queue and PD prompt-length bucketing - config-profile `promptTokensGte` / `promptTokensLt` matching This matches what the engine actually processes, but tool-heavy traffic will land in larger buckets than before. Requests that share a large tool set now also share a long leading prefix and are therefore more likely to stay on the same pods, as the engine cache would suggest. **Tests** (`prefix_tools_test.go`): - absent, `null` and `[]` tools produce exactly the old output - OpenAI and Anthropic tool shapes render to the expected canonical text - different tools drop the prefix-index match below 50%, while an identical repeat still matches 100% - 50 seeded key-order and whitespace permutations produce one text - characters are not HTML-escaped - `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_INCLUDE_TOOLS=false` restores the old output - invalid `tools` fall back to the raw bytes Verification: - `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/ ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/...` passes - golangci-lint reports no issues ## Related Issues Resolves: #2782 **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [Bug] Recover panics in the queue router serve loop
[Bug] Key PD router per-pod load state by namespace/name
body:
## Pull Request Description The PD router's per-pod load state lives on the single `pdRouter` instance and is shared across every model and namespace. It was keyed by the bare pod name, however, so same-named pods in two namespaces merged their accounting: each pod carried the other's token load and in-flight counts, and they shared one metric series. This PR keys that state by `namespace/name`. - The three router-level trackers now key by `namespace/name`, the same format as `utils.GeneratePodKey` and the key the gateway cache already uses for per-pod state: - `TokenLoadTracker` - `PrefillRequestTracker` - `PendingDecodeTracker` The tracker APIs still take a string, now documented as the pod key. Releases look up by request ID, and the key recorded when a charge is taken is reused on release, so charges cannot be released under a different key form. - A new `pd.PodKey(pod)` helper builds the key with plain concatenation, byte-identical to `utils.GeneratePodKey`, which a test asserts. It avoids adding `fmt.Sprintf` calls inside the `selectMu` critical section. - The `pd_token_load_active_tokens` and `pd_token_load_kv_tokens` gauges gain a `namespace` label, following the separate namespace/pod labels of the other per-pod gateway metrics. - `pod_name` keeps the bare pod name, so existing queries and the e2e scrape keep working. - The janitor's idle-pod pruning deletes the series with the same label values it set. - Tracker log lines use `pod=` instead of `pod_name`. - Left as is: `matchedPods` and the per-request score maps, including the map returned by `GetPrefillRequestCountsForPods`, stay keyed by pod name. The prefix match comes from the per-model prefix index shared with the `prefix_cache` router. A single model name served from two namespaces can still put two same-named pods into one candidate list. That problem predates this change and is out of scope here. `BenchmarkFilterPrefillDecodePods`, 8 prefill + 8 decode pods, `-benchmem -count=6`: | | least_request | prefix_cache | |---|---|---| | main | ~21.3–22.5 µs, 232 allocs | ~72.7–74.4 µs, 240 allocs | | this PR | ~21.0–21.3 µs, 218 allocs | ~72.7–73.2 µs, 226 allocs | Tests: - same-named pods in two namespaces keep separate token-load counters, gauge series and pruning (`TestTokenLoadTracker_SameNameInTwoNamespaces`) - token_load scores stay independent (`TestTokenLoadPrefillPolicy_SameNameInTwoNamespaces`) - the prefill and decode request trackers keep separate counts (`TestRequestTrackers_SameNameInTwoNamespaces`) - `PodKey` matches `GeneratePodKey` - existing tests are updated to pod keys Verification: - `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/` passes - `go vet ./test/e2e/...` passes - golangci-lint reports no issues ## Related Issues Resolves: #2783 **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [Gateway] Score load-balance on output-token rate, committed work, and KV pressure
body:
## Pull Request Description Replace the request drain-rate capacity in the load-balance router with score = (running + λ·queued) / EWMA(output tokens/sec) × (1 + α·(1 − kvFree)²) and route to the lowest score. Capacity (observed token throughput), load (committed work) and KV headroom are now separate inputs, so a saturated replica is no longer read as "send it more traffic" and request size no longer skews the capacity estimate on heterogeneous hardware. - Cache: count output tokens completed per pod (gateway-tracked, engine agnostic, carried across pod delete/re-add like completedRequests) and publish RealtimeOutputTokenRateEWMA: the 1-minute token rate smoothed with a 10s time constant. A window with no completed tokens keeps the previous estimate instead of decaying it, so a briefly idle pod is not starved. - Router: pods with no estimate yet are scored at the mean of the measured pods (a fixed 1.0 would be off by the tokens/sec scale and lock a new pod out). A pod below the critical free-KV fraction scores +Inf; if every pod is below it the request still routes to the pod with the most KV headroom. - New knobs: AIBRIX_LOAD_BALANCE_QUEUED_WEIGHT (default 0, since the running count already includes engine-queued requests), _KV_PRESSURE_ALPHA (2.0) and _KV_CRITICAL_FREE (0.10). - The PD decode path keeps its own request drain-rate scoring. - Add load_balance.md, update the router docs and ENV_VARS.md, migrate the load-balance unit and gateway integration tests, and add tests for the score, the KV guardrail, unmeasured pods, and the cache counter/EWMA. ## Related Issues Resolves: #[Insert issue number(s)] **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [Misc] Add queue observability metrics to the gateway SLO queue
body:
## Pull Request Description

The gateway's SLO queue (`routingAlgorithm=slo`) is invisible on the metrics surface: nothing reports how long a request waits for a slot, how deep the queue runs, how requests leave it, or whether the queue is serving FIFO because no profile was usable. This adds four metrics around the queue, emitted from the request path itself:

| Metric | Type | Extra label | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `gateway_queue_wait_time_bucket_total` | Counter | `bucket` | Time from enqueue to leaving the queue |
| `gateway_queue_pending_requests` | Gauge | - | Current queue depth for the model |
| `gateway_queue_outcome_total` | Counter | `outcome` | How the request left: `routed`, `slo_failure`, `capacity_reached`, `error` |
| `gateway_queue_fifo_fallback_total` | Counter | `reason` | Dispatches served by the FIFO fallback: `no_profile`, `no_slo_info` |

Wait time is stamped on the routing context when the request is enqueued (`RoutingContext.QueueStartTime`), so the bucket measures residency in the queue rather than time since arrival; a context that was never stamped falls back to `RequestTime`. The bucket bounds (10ms to 60s) are coarser than the request-path duration buckets because a request can wait tens of seconds for capacity, and they follow the existing label convention (`low-highms`, `Nms+`) instead of introducing a histogram.

`outcome` is classified with `errors.Is`, so wrapped errors still land in the right bucket: `ErrorSLOFailureRequest` -> `slo_failure`, `ErrorLoadCapacityReached` -> `capacity_reached`, anything else -> `error`. The FIFO fallback is recorded where the decision is made: `SLOQueue.Peek` marks the fallback candidate with its reason and `Dequeue` counts it once.

All four are emitted with the same low-cardinality label set as the other gateway request metrics (`model`, `lora_adapter`, `gateway_pod`) and never with pod labels, keeping the cardinality direction discussed in #2569; the pod that serves the request is already covered by the per-pod request metrics. Pending depth is set (`Set(Len())`) after enqueue and after dequeue rather than incremented and decremented, so an error between the two cannot drift the gauge.

Tests: `TestQueueWaitBucketLabel` pins the bucket bounds, `TestQueueOutcomeLabel` pins the four outcomes (including a wrapped error), `TestQueueMetricsRegistered` guards against a metric being dropped silently because it is missing from the registry, and `TestQueueRouterEmitsQueueMetricsByOutcome` drives a `queueRouter` end to end with a fake queue and backend for the four outcomes, checking the emitted labels and the pending sequence `1 -> 0`. The SLOQueue fallback reasons are covered by two ginkgo specs plus a ranked-candidate control case.

`gofmt` and `go vet` are clean; `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/types/... ./pkg/metrics/...` and `go test -race` on the two touched packages pass.

## Related Issues

Related to: #2569 (low-cardinality direction for gateway metrics).

title: [Feat] Recover panics on the gateway plugin request path
body:
## Pull Request Description

The plugin had no panic recovery on the ExtProc path: `grpc.NewServer` in `cmd/plugins/main.go` is built with the OTel stats handler and a max message size and nothing else, so one panic in the stream handler ends the whole `aibrix-gateway-plugins` process together with every request in flight on it. #2756 hit exactly that on the routing path (a malformed profile making `ModelGPUProfile.GetSignature` panic); #1284 (index out of range in the queue) and #2049 (pod restarts under high concurrency) have the same blast radius on the same path.

This recovers at the server boundary, with no new dependency:

```go
opts = append(opts, grpc.StreamInterceptor(gateway.StreamPanicRecoveryInterceptor()))
```

A recovered panic logs the stack trace, counts a new `gateway_request_panic_total` counter, and fails only the stream it happened on with `codes.Internal`. The panic value stays in the log and the reply only names the method, the way other internal errors on the request path are reported.

Both questions from the issue are answered by the change: the stream interceptor is the primary home because it covers every handler on that server, and the `Process` defer stays as the fallback for callers that never go through the transport. The metric follows the existing gateway naming, pod-scoped with the `pod_name` label, since no constraint was recorded. A handler error is passed through unchanged rather than being rewritten as a panic.

Verified by:
- a real gRPC server with the interceptor registered: the stream whose handler panics ends with `codes.Internal`, and a second stream on the same server still runs;
- reverting the interceptor locally: the same test dies with the raw `panic: boom in Process`, which is the blast radius this PR removes;
- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/metrics/...`, `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/ ./pkg/metrics/`, `go vet` and `gofmt` clean.

Recovery is a last line of defense, not a replacement for fixing the defect, and it cannot catch runtime-fatal conditions such as concurrent map writes or OOM.

## Related Issues

Resolves: #2759

title: [Bug] Enforce tokenizer pool capacity during concurrent creation
body:
## Pull Request Description

Two concurrent requests for different models can both pass `TokenizerPool`'s capacity check, perform their health checks outside the lock, and then insert into the last available slot. A pool configured for one tokenizer can therefore retain two. The initial capacity check also prevents replacing an unhealthy tokenizer when the pool is full, even though replacing that model needs no additional slot.

Recheck capacity while holding the insertion lock and allow same-model replacements. Close clients discarded after a failed health check or a lost capacity race, and close the unhealthy client when replacing it.

The regression tests use a local HTTP server and a channel barrier to force both creations past their initial checks before allowing either to finish. They cover different-model capacity contention, same-model deduplication, recovery at capacity, and idle-connection cleanup.

## Related Issues

No existing issue. Checked all-state tokenizer/pool PRs and issues for overlapping work.

## Validation

- On unmodified main with the regression tests added: capacity contention, unhealthy replacement, and failed-health-check cleanup fail; same-model deduplication passes.
- `go test -tags=nozmq ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms ./pkg/utils/tokenizer -count=1` — passed.
- `go test -race -tags=nozmq ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms -run '^TestTokenizerPool' -count=1` — passed.
- `go vet -tags=nozmq ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms ./pkg/utils/tokenizer` — passed.
- `gofmt` and `git diff --check` — passed.

Validated with Go 1.26.0 on Windows/amd64, using the existing `nozmq` build tag. No live inference service or Kubernetes cluster was needed; cluster E2E and ZeroMQ integration were not run.

title: fix(kvcache): decode vLLM map-format KV events; tier-aware prefix scoring
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2285. While investigating, I found a larger compatibility break:
vLLM switched KV event encoding from positional arrays to **msgpack maps** in
[vllm-project/vllm#42892](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/42892)
(merged 2026-06-09). `DecodeEventBatch` still expected `[ts, events]` arrays,
so **every** KV event payload from current vLLM fails to unmarshal
(`msgpack: invalid code=0x88 decoding array length`) — kv-events prefix
routing is effectively dead against current vLLM. The legacy publisher also
sent one event per ZMQ message (tag-first array), which the batch-shaped
decoder never handled either.

## Changes

- `pkg/cache/kvcache/msgpack_decoder.go`: accept all three wire shapes —
  map single event (current vLLM), tag-first array single event (legacy
  vLLM), and `[ts, events]` batch (older code paths / test encoder).
- Parse every `BlockStored`/`BlockRemoved` field: `lora_id`, `medium`,
  `lora_name`, `extra_keys`, `group_idx`, `kv_cache_spec_kind`,
  `kv_cache_spec_sliding_window`, `locality`.
- `pkg/utils/syncprefixcacheindexer`: record the storage `medium` per
  (prefix, pod) and weight `MatchPrefix` scores (GPU=1.0, CPU=0.5,
  STORAGE=0.25; unspecified keeps full score for backward compatibility)
  so pods holding a prefix only on a slower tier are not over-credited.
- Plumb `medium`/`lora_name`/`group_idx` through the `kvevent` handler and
  `store_providers` adapter (previously dropped at the handler).

## Tests

New `decoder_vllm_compat_test.go` verifies decoding against **byte-exact
payloads generated with the real msgspec encoder** for both current map and
legacy array formats (single-event and batch shapes). New
`medium_scoring_test.go` covers tier weighting via `AddPrefixWithMedium` and
the event ingestion path. All existing `kvcache` and
`syncprefixcacheindexer` tests keep passing.

## Follow-up

The `(model, lora_name, group_idx)` index keying part of #2285 needs a
request-side adapter id (`RoutingContext` has no LoRA field today); see the
issue thread.

title: [Bug] Repin the session-affinity Redis pin on a bypassed final target
body:
## Pull Request Description `sessionAffinityRouter.PostRouteUpdate` is called on paths that bypass `Route`/`resolveSessionPod` (the multi-strategy router's single-remaining-candidate fast path, and blended commits). Before this change, it always persisted the final target pod with the non-destructive claim write (Redis `SET NX`). If Redis already held a *different* address for that session key (for example, a load-imbalance gate had excluded the previously-pinned pod so routing moved to a different one), the `SET NX` was silently rejected and Redis kept the stale address indefinitely, even though the response's `x-session-id` header and the proxied request already pointed at the new pod. This adds `commitFinalTarget`, which first observes the pinning already recorded for the session key (from the local cache when it's confirmed, otherwise a fresh Redis read) and, when that differs from the final target, repins atomically via a small Lua compare-and-swap (`sessionKeyRepinScript`): it swaps the observed old address for the new one, attaches the new address if the key had expired, and otherwise leaves a different value (a fresher concurrent repin by another replica) untouched, converging this replica's local cache onto whichever address actually won. When the observation already matches the final target, or there's nothing to preserve, the existing non-destructive claim write handles it unchanged. Out of scope, left as-is: `resolveSessionPod`'s own `writeRepin` mode (used when replacing a stale local/Redis entry with a fresh rendezvous pick) still does an unconditional `SET`; that's a separate call site the issue didn't report and this PR doesn't touch. ## Validation - `go build ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...` - `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/...` - `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/... -run TestSessionAffinity -v` — all 24 cases pass, including a rewritten regression test (`TestSessionAffinityPostRouteUpdateRepinsExistingPin`, replacing one that asserted the old, buggy "must not overwrite" contract), two new tests for the CAS script's own outcomes (`TestSessionAffinityRepinLeavesFresherConcurrentWinnerAlone`, `TestSessionAffinityRepinAttachesExpiredKey`), and a nil-Redis regression test (`TestSessionAffinityPostRouteUpdateNoRedisDoesNotPanic`). - `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/...` and `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/utils/...` both pass. - `golangci-lint run ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/...` reports only a pre-existing, unrelated gofmt finding in `pd_bucketing_test.go` that is present on `main` without this change (confirmed via `git stash`). I did not run the deployed two-gateway load-gate reproduction described in the issue (no live cluster in this environment); the targeted unit tests above reproduce the same defect directly: the rewritten test fails against the old code (Redis keeps the stale address) and passes against this fix. ## Related Issues Resolves: #2772 **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [Bug] Gate the session-affinity Redis refresh on the stored value
body:
## Pull Request Description

The Redis write-through for session-key pinning still refreshed with an unconditional `SET`: a TTL refresh for an old address that landed after another replica had repinned the session silently wrote the old address back, reverting the newer pinning, and it also pushed out the TTL of whatever value was stored by the time it ran.

This gates the refresh on the stored value through a small Lua script that compares and writes in one atomic step:

```go
var sessionKeyRefreshScript = redis.NewScript(`
local current = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
if not current then
  redis.call('SET', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], 'PX', tonumber(ARGV[2]))
  return {2}
end
if current == ARGV[1] then
  redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[2]))
  return {1}
end
return {0, current}
`)
```

The TTL is extended when the stored value still matches `addr`, the pin is re-attached with a fresh TTL when the key is missing (so an actively used session cannot lose its affinity right at the expiry boundary, and nothing can be overwritten), and nothing is written when the key holds a different address. On that mismatch the script returns the stored value with the outcome, so the refresh converges the local entry on the exact value that rejected it, without a second read that could miss a key expiring in between, even a confirmed entry, since the refresh just established that Redis no longer vouches for it, the same way a lost claim already converges; the stale replica therefore follows the newer pin instead of routing from the old address until the next sync pass. A Lua script rather than GET followed by SET/EXPIRE is used because the gate has to hold against concurrent writers; it goes through `redis.NewScript`, so refreshes on the hot path run by EVALSHA once the server has it cached, matching the pattern already used for the gateway's async-job scripts. A reply the script cannot emit is treated as a failure rather than a confirmation. Failover repins keep the unconditional write; their compare-and-swap is the remaining follow-up recorded in the TODO.

This is the refresh half of the write-semantics feedback from the #2742 review (discussion_r4037407790), split out after the claim half (#2765) merged. Say the word if you would rather see the remaining repin CAS folded in here instead.

Verified by reverting the fix locally: with the gated refresh replaced by the plain SET, the new regression spec fails with `10.0.0.1:8000` reappearing over the repinned `10.0.0.2:8000` and its TTL being extended; with the fix it passes. `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, and `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/utils/...` all pass.

## Related Issues

Related issue: N/A. Implements the TTL-refresh race from the write-semantics feedback in the #2742 review (discussion_r4037407790); the claim half landed in #2765.

title: [API][ModelClaim] Admit placement against a declared per-GPU cost
body:
## Pull Request Description The controller picks a warm pod, spawns the engine, and only finds out the model does not fit when the engine runs out of memory. By then the claim has spent its restart budget on that one pod, and placement does not try another. Free HBM cannot answer "will this fit" on its own. Free memory is not room. It is only memory nobody has touched yet. It does not include memory already promised to an instance whose engine is still loading, which takes tens of seconds, and it moves with traffic once the engine is serving. So a claim declares what one instance costs on one card, and placement keeps an account rather than reading free memory. ## What a claim declares ```yaml spec: perGPU: maximumFootprint: 30Gi kvFloor: 10Gi ``` Neither figure can be derived from the artifact. Most of the gap between an artifact and what an engine holds is allocator retention, which does not scale with the weights, so both come from a run of this model with these engine arguments. Declaring more than an instance needs wastes room and is safe. Declaring less is not. They are quantities rather than byte counts, because nobody checks `32212254720` by eye. Both are currently required, so a claim without them is rejected at `kubectl apply`. That stops a new claim from being admitted without a cost, and it does not clean up after one: a claim stored before the field existed still decodes with it missing, still leaves its card unaccountable, and has to be rewritten by hand. Whether required is the right first landing is open, and is being settled in #2744 along with the shape of the field itself. ## What the control plane works out | Name | Source | What it is | |---|---|---| | `hbmUsableBytes` | measured by the runtime | NVML v2 total, less what the driver reserves. Per card, measured once. | | `minimumReserveBytes` | derived | `maximumFootprint + kvFloor`. What one instance takes and does not give back while it is awake, asleep included. | | `maximumRoomBytes` | derived | `hbmUsableBytes` less every recorded instance's `maximumFootprint + kvFloor`. The most this card could ever offer. | An instance is charged from the moment it is recorded in `status`, not from the moment its engine gets around to allocating, so an activating instance is never invisible to the next admission. Status alone is not enough to judge a card, though. It says what this controller committed; the snapshot says what is actually running. An engine in the snapshot that no recorded instance answers for is memory nobody is accounting for. Free memory used to cover that by accident, because an engine holding memory showed up as memory not free. Nothing here reads free memory, so the card is refused instead. ## The decision ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Claim to place
minimumReserveBytes =
maximumFootprint + kvFloor"] --> B{"Can this card
be accounted for?"} B -- "no: runtime silent, card unmeasured,
a claim there declares nothing,
or an engine answers to no claim" --> R1["Refuse: cannot judge this card"] B -- yes --> C{"Is maximumRoomBytes at least
minimumReserveBytes?"} C -- no --> R2["Refuse: this card cannot hold it"] C -- yes --> E["Admit, rank by room, start the engine"] R1 --> W["No card admits it: stay Pending
and try again on the next pass"] R2 --> W ``` Ranking follows the same account. It used to order the admitted pods by free memory, which is the signal this change argues is not room, so two cards that both fit were ordered by something that moves with traffic. The roomiest card still wins. Packing onto the tightest card that fits is a separate decision and is not taken here. The refusal names the roomiest pod that still could not hold the model, which is the smallest gap to close: ``` no warm pod can hold this model, which needs 40.0 GiB on a card: warm-runtime-pool-zeyu-... can offer at most 15.3 GiB ``` `Scheduled` is set to `True` with reason `Placed` once an instance is recorded. Before this, the condition was only ever set to `False`, so a claim turned away once carried that refusal for the rest of its life. ## What this change does not do The account is a reservation in the control plane and not in the hardware. Nothing here stops an engine already on the card from growing its KV cache into the space held for another instance, and every engine still runs under whatever limit its KV allocator chose for itself. Holding an engine to a limit is the next change in this line of work, and the feature page says so rather than leaving it to be discovered. Sleeping does not free a seat either. An instance that is asleep keeps its place in the account at the full declared cost, because the assignment has to survive the sleep for a wake to find its engine again. Sleep can give KV back to the models beside it; it cannot make room for a new claim. ## Checked on hardware The figures come from a run on one H20 with the whole of this line of work applied, not this change alone. What it shows about this change: the runtime measured the card at 95.33 GiB usable, two 1.5B models each declaring a 30Gi footprint and a 10Gi floor were both admitted and served, and a third claim of the same size was refused with no engine started for it. The cases that are awkward to stage on a real pool are covered by unit tests: a runtime that does not answer, a card the runtime could not measure, a pod carrying a claim that declares nothing, and a pod running an engine that no recorded instance answers for are each refused rather than admitted. ## Related Issues Related: #2744, which proposes a single optional `requiredHBMBytesPerGPU` filtered against observed free HBM. The difference between the two shapes, and whether the field should be required on its first landing, are being discussed there. Only one of them should land. Related: #2770, which is why the declaration cannot be checked against observation yet: `hbm_peak_bytes` reads 0 for every engine, because NVML reports host PIDs and the runtime walks the container's process tree. Replaces the earlier version of this PR, which measured the footprint itself and stored it in `status`. That approach is gone, along with the three blockers raised against it.

title: [Bug] Purge a pod's prefix cache when the engine sleep-state metric shows it went to sleep
body:
Closes #2287.

This grew from what it started as. Original scope was just the metric label-filtering bug below; the tracker and edge-triggered purge (the actual backstop) turned out to be ready sooner than the original PR description said to expect, so it's in the same PR now rather than a follow-up.

## The bug this fixes

`vllm:engine_sleep_state` reports one gauge family with three instances per pod, distinguished only by the `sleep_state` label (`awake`, `weights_offloaded`, `discard_all`), each its own 0/1 series. Nothing in the Prometheus exposition format guarantees scrape order, but `parseMetricFromFamily` read `metricFamily.Metric[0]` unconditionally, so which of the three series aibrix actually recorded depended on whatever order that particular scrape happened to return.

Added `Metric.RequiredLabelKey`/`RequiredLabelValue`: when set, `parseMetricFromFamily` searches the family for the instance whose label matches instead of taking the first one. Every other registered metric leaves this unset and keeps the exact `Metric[0]` behavior it has today. `EngineSleepState` now filters to `sleep_state=awake`.

## The backstop

The `AllBlocksCleared` ZMQ event handler already purges a pod's prefix cache on `/reset_prefix_cache`, OOM-driven reset, or `/sleep`. It's not complete: vLLM only flushes queued KV events from inside a scheduler step, so an idle or sleeping engine may never emit one, and ZMQ delivery is lossy. The pod stays `Running` with `/health` returning 200, so the prefix router keeps preferring it for prefixes whose blocks are gone.

`Manager.CheckSleepStateBackstop` reads the (now correctly filtered) `engine_sleep_state` value already scraped every refresh tick and purges on the awake-to-asleep transition, per (pod, model). Edge triggered, not level triggered: `RemovePrefix` takes the prefix router's write lock and is O(P) in cached prefixes for the model, so purging on every tick a sleeping pod is observed would hold that lock once per refresh interval for as long as it stays asleep. A (pod, model) pair with no prior observation is seeded as having been awake, so a gateway restart while a pod is already asleep still self-corrects on the first observation.

`Manager.PurgePodPrefixCache` factors the get-indexer-then-`RemovePrefix` logic the event handler already had into a method the backstop also calls, so a pod's cache is purged the same way whether aibrix learned about it from a ZMQ event or from this metric. `unsubscribeFromPod` now also forgets the pod's tracked sleep state, so a reused pod key is seeded fresh.

Wired into `pkg/cache`'s existing `worker()` metrics loop, right where `engine_sleep_state` is already read for Prometheus export. No new scraping. `KVEventManager.CheckSleepStateBackstop` is a no-op in the default (non-zmq) build, matching every other `KVEventManager` method: the backstop needs the sync indexer KV event sync provides.

## Verification

- `go build` and `go vet` clean under both the default and `zmq` build tags, across the whole module
- This sandbox's own `go test` harness aborts on an unrelated dyld error, reproduced against the unmodified branch too, so verified by running the compiled test binaries directly instead: the full `pkg/kvevent` suite (26 tests, 7 new for the backstop) and the full `pkg/cache` suite (`zmq`-tagged) both pass, zero regressions
- Mutation-tested the awake-seeding behavior specifically: removing it makes the seeding test fail as expected

title: [API] Add an authoritative model routing policy
body:
## Pull Request Description

This change adds an opt-in `authoritativeRoutingPolicy` field to the existing `model.aibrix.ai/config` annotation.

When the policy is enabled, the model configuration becomes authoritative for request routing:

- The configured `defaultProfile` is used instead of an application-supplied named or `auto` `config-profile`.
- An application-supplied `routing-strategy` cannot override the configured routing strategy.
- An application-supplied `external-filter` cannot change the eligible Pod set.
- Gateway-generated routing information and request mutations are preserved internally.
- The gateway omits `routing-strategy`, `target-pod`, `target-pod-ip`, and `x-aibrix-config-profile` from the response.

The field defaults to `false`, so existing deployments retain their current request-header precedence and response behavior.

This complements the `lockedRoutingStrategy` support added by #2544. The existing field pins the routing algorithm, while `authoritativeRoutingPolicy` also protects profile parameters and replica selection from request-level overrides.

The change includes documentation and regression coverage for:

- Named and automatic configuration profiles.
- Default-profile routing parameters.
- Locked routing algorithms.
- Matching and nonmatching external filters.
- Preservation of gateway-generated routing information.
- Suppression of routing diagnostic response headers.
- Backward-compatible behavior when the policy is disabled.

### Testing

The following checks passed:

- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/configprofiles -run 'TestResolveConfigForRequest' -count=1`
- `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway -run 'Test(ApplyConfigProfile|DeriveRoutingStrategyFromContext|HandleRequestBody_LockedRoutingStrategy|_HandleResponseHeaders)' -count=1`

A gateway image built with the `zmq` feature was also validated in a local Kind deployment. The deployed matrix covered baseline requests and requests containing valid, invalid, and mixed-case `routing-strategy` values; named and automatic `config-profile` values; matching and nonmatching `external-filter` values; and a combined adversarial request.

All requests completed successfully. The configured routing policy remained effective, gateway-generated routing information was preserved internally, and the routing diagnostic headers were omitted from responses.

title: [Bug] Stop LocalStorage rewriting newlines in stored text objects
body:
## The bug

`LocalStorage._write_file` writes text objects through a text-mode handle:

```python
with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(str(reader))
```

Without `newline=""`, Python translates every `"\n"` written to `os.linesep`. On Windows that means a stored text object comes back with `\r\n`, so `put_object(x)` followed by `get_object()` does not return `x`. Nothing raises — the corruption is silent, and `LocalStorage` is the default local-development backend.

Minimal repro, independent of aibrix:

```python
fd, p = tempfile.mkstemp()
with os.fdopen(fd, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write("a\nb")
open(p, "rb").read()      # b'a\r\nb' on Windows, b'a\nb' with newline=""
```

## Why it has gone unnoticed

`os.linesep` is `"\n"` on Linux, so the translation is a no-op there and CI stays green. It is only observable on Windows, where it already makes an existing spec fail:

```
tests/storage/test_reader.py::TestReaderIntegration::test_reader_with_different_file_types_in_storage
AssertionError: assert b'name,age\r\nAlice,30\r\nBob,25' == b'name,age\nAlice,30\nBob,25'
```

## The fix

Pass `newline=""` so the bytes are written exactly as given. That is the standard way to ask Python for no newline translation — the same thing the `csv` module's docs require when opening files.

Scope is deliberately one line. `_write_json_file` uses the same text-mode pattern but is not affected: `json.dump` emits no bare newlines and escapes `\n` inside values, so nothing reaches the translation layer. Happy to harden it defensively in a follow-up if maintainers prefer.

## Tests

Added `test_text_content_round_trips_without_newline_translation`, which stores a string containing `\n`, reads it back, and asserts the bytes are unchanged. Removing `newline=""` again turns it red on Windows with a diagnostic failure:

```
assert b'first\r\nsecond\r\nthird' == b'first\nsecond\nthird'
```

**One honest limitation:** this spec cannot fail on Linux CI, for the same reason the bug is invisible there. I could not find a way to catch it on Linux without asserting on the implementation (e.g. mocking `os.fdopen` and checking the arguments), which seemed worse than leaving it platform-gated. The structural answer is Windows coverage in CI, which is beyond this PR — flagging it rather than pretending the spec guards every platform.

With the fix, `pytest tests/storage` is 156 passed / 13 skipped on Windows; previously 154 passed / 1 failed.

title: [Misc] Add unit tests for the RoundRobin dispatch policy

Both pass.

title: [Bug] Use SET NX for the initial session-affinity Redis claim
body:
## Pull Request Description

The Redis write-through for session-key pinning shares one unconditional `SET` across three cases with different concurrency-safety needs: the initial claim, TTL-only refreshes, and failover repins. That leaves the initial claim racy: two gateway replicas that both miss Redis and resolve different pods for the same session can overwrite each other's pinning (last writer wins), and an unconfirmed sync-pass retry can replace a pinning that another replica already owns.

This makes the claim atomic instead: `persistSessionKeyToRedis` now takes the caller's write intent, and the claim persists with `SET NX EX`:

```go
if mode == writeClaim {
	claimed, err := r.redisClient.SetNX(ctx, sessionAffinityRedisKey(cacheKey), addr, sessionAffinityTTL).Result()
	if err != nil {
		klog.V(4).ErrorS(err, "failed to persist session key pinning to redis", "cache_key", cacheKey)
		return false
	}
	if !claimed {
		return false
	}
	r.markSessionKeyConfirmed(cacheKey, addr)
	return true
}
```

A fresh rendezvous pick on the route path, the sync-pass retry, an unconfirmed local-cache hit, and the post-route commit (the single-ready-pod fast path and blended commits) all use this claim mode. A lost claim reads the winner back and converges the local entry on it, so the losing replica follows the winner on its next request instead of waiting for the sync pass. Refresh and repin intentionally keep the unconditional write for now. Gating a refresh on the stored value still matching `addr` (so a delayed refresh cannot revert a newer repin) and a compare-and-swap for repins are the follow-ups recorded in the TODO at the call site, and the write-intent plumbing added here is what those build on. Say the word if you would rather see those folded into a single larger change instead.

Verified by reverting each part of the fix locally: the added specs fail with the losing replica's address replacing the existing pinning (`10.0.0.2:8000` landing over `10.0.0.1:8000`), and pass with the fix. `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/`, and `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/... ./pkg/cache/...` all pass.

## Related Issues

Related issue: N/A. Implements the first step of the write-semantics feedback from the #2742 review (discussion_r4037407790).

title: [Misc] Fix misleading SLOQueue fallback log message
body:
## Pull Request Description

The per-request warning in `SLOQueue.Peek` claims the request would "fallback to FIFO queue" when no deployment profile can rank it. That is not the code path: the request is only excluded from this round's ranking, and the FIFO fallback candidate is used only when no candidate can be ranked at all. Whenever other ranked candidates remain, the message misstates the routing decision.

Rephrase the message to match the actual behavior, note in the fallback handler comment when the fallback candidate is used, and fix two `ealiest` typos in nearby comments. No behavior change; the FIFO fallback path itself is untouched.

Verified locally: `gofmt -l pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/` is clean, and `go vet ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/`, `go build ./...`, `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/ -count=1` (also with `-race`) all pass.

title: [Feat] Add Redis-backed session-key pinning for cross-replica agentic routing
body:
## Pull Request Description Adds Redis-backed session-key pinning so `session-affinity` can keep concurrent agentic requests on the same inference pod across gateway replicas, plus follow-up correctness fixes so that stickiness actually holds after scale-out, cache isolation, and blend behavior. ### Agentic routing `x-session-id` only works after the first response comes back, which is too late for agentic workloads that fan out concurrent tool calls or sub-agent requests. Callers can now send a stable `x-aibrix-session-key` from the first request: - Sequential multi-turn chat still uses the gateway-issued `x-session-id`. - Concurrent/agentic requests use a caller-owned `x-aibrix-session-key` (conversation ID, agent-run ID, etc.). - With `REDIS_HOST` configured, the key→pod pinning is shared across gateway replicas (1-hour sliding TTL). Without Redis, mapping stays deterministic via rendezvous hashing over the current ready pod set. - Keys longer than 256 bytes are treated as unset and fall back to normal session-affinity resolution. - The same header can be reused by PD `token_load` / `hybrid_cache_load` policies. Docs: `docs/source/features/agentic-routing.rst`. ### Correctness Follow-ups - **Drop the session-affinity load-balance auto-blend:** Session-affinity `ScoreAll` is binary (1 for the resolved pod, 0 elsewhere), so the previous 5:4 blend could never be overridden by load-balance disagreement. Bare `session-affinity` now runs unblended, like `pd` / `slo*` / standalone `load-balance`. Prefix-cache keeps the 5:4 ratio because its scoring is graded. - **Honor stickiness on the single-ready-pod fast path:** `selectTargetPod` used to return that pod without calling `router.Route()`, so a session started while only one pod was ready never got a Redis pin or `x-session-id` header. After scale-out, rendezvous hashing could move the session. The router's `PostRouteUpdate` hook now runs on that path, including through `multiStrategyRouter`. - **Isolate and bound the session-key cache:** Redis/local cache keys are scoped by model (`sessionCacheKey`) so two models sharing Redis — or a reused session-key value — don't overwrite each other. The local `sessionKeyPods` cache is capped by `AIBRIX_SESSION_AFFINITY_MAX_LOCAL_KEYS` (default 100k); past the cap, new keys still resolve via Redis or rendezvous hashing. - **Harden Lookup / local-cache races:** `Lookup` rejects a nil provider instead of dereferencing it. `storeSessionKeyLocal` uses a `LoadOrStore` / `CompareAndSwap` retry loop so concurrent writes can't clobber a newer pinning or un-confirm one whose Redis write already landed. > **Note / Known Leftover:** `persistSessionKeyToRedis`'s unconditional `SET` is shared by initial-claim, TTL-refresh, and failover-repin writes and can still race across gateway replicas. title: [Bug] Keep ranked candidates in SLOQueue when a rank lookup fails
body:
## Pull Request Description

One failed profile ranking made `SLOQueue.Peek` drop every ranked candidate and serve the earliest request in FIFO order. The rank error was stored in a variable shared by the whole scan, and after the scan the candidate list was truncated to the first (FIFO fallback) entry; a profile that cannot rank a single request, for example one whose index table does not cover the request signature, therefore collapsed the routing decision for all subqueues.

`rankImpl` already reports per-profile errors and `Peek` logs a warning for them, so this finishes that contract:

```go
if rankErr != nil {
	klog.Warningf("SLOQueue failed to get SLO info for request %s with profile %s: %v, skip.", r.RequestID, profile.Deployment, rankErr)
	continue
}
```

Candidates whose profiles all fail are removed from the ranked list instead of taking part in the cross-candidate sort. A subqueue with no rankable profiles still falls back to FIFO; I left that path unchanged, so say the word if you would rather revisit it.

Verified by reverting the fix locally: two of the added specs fail and return the FIFO candidate (`req-early` / `req-waiting`) instead of the most urgent ranked candidate; removing only the candidate cleanup makes the all-fail spec panic in the sort with `index out of range [0] with length 0`. With the fix, `go test -race ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/` and `go test ./pkg/plugins/gateway/...` pass.

## Related Issues

Related issue: N/A. Found while reviewing the rank failure path that #2756 also guards.

title: [Gateway] Fail the client request and abort the decode leg when the SGLang PD prefill leg fails
body:
## Pull Request Description In SGLang PD disaggregation the gateway fires the prefill leg asynchronously and lets Envoy forward the decode leg. When the prefill leg fails (dead prefill pod, non-2xx, timeout, client cancel) nothing tells the decode pod or the client: the decode pod sits in its bootstrap / prealloc queue for that `bootstrap_room` until the engine's own bootstrap timeout (minutes), holding a decode slot, and the client sees a long hang followed by an opaque decode-side error. This is #2289. This PR keeps the prefill dispatch asynchronous (the constraint raised in #2289) and only stops discarding its result. ### What changes 1. **`utils.LoadEnvNonNegativeInt`** — `LoadEnvInt` treats every value ≤ 0 as invalid and silently falls back, so a knob whose documented value `0` means "off" cannot be switched off from the environment. The new helper accepts 0 and still refuses negative/unparseable values. `LoadEnvInt` is unchanged for its callers. 2. **Gateway-owned `rid` + decode abort on prefill failure.** SGLang's `/abort_request` matches on `rid` only (`AbortReq` has no room field) and reads `rid` from the request body, not from `X-Request-Id`. The gateway now writes `rid = -<16-hex nonce>` into both legs' bodies (fixed width because SGLang's abort match is prefix based; the nonce keeps retries with a reused request id distinct). When the async prefill leg fails, the failure is classified (`http_status`, `timeout`, `canceled`, `transport`, `request_setup`, `bad_response`) and the gateway POSTs `{"rid": ...}` to the decode pod's `/abort_request`. The abort is best-effort on its own goroutine with its own timeout, sent twice (immediately and after a short delay) because a prefill pod that refuses the connection outright lets the first abort overtake the decode leg, and the tokenizer manager silently drops an abort for an unknown rid. It is skipped once the decode pod has started responding. `bad_response` (HTTP 200 with an unparseable body) never aborts because the transfer did complete. 3. **Fail the client request immediately.** `Route()` only produces the header mutation, but the same ext_proc stream stays open for the response and is parked in `srv.Recv()` waiting for decode response headers that will not arrive until the bootstrap timeout. `srv.Recv()` moves into one reader goroutine per stream and the processing loop becomes a `select` over the reader, the stream context and a per-request prefill-failure wakeup. Non-PD streams select on exactly the two cases they had before. When a terminal prefill failure lands before the decode pod has responded, the gateway answers with an `ImmediateResponse` (503 for timeout/transport/request_setup/canceled, the upstream status for `http_status`, 502 otherwise) carrying an OpenAI-shaped error body and `x-error-pd-prefill: true`, then closes the stream with a gRPC error so `failure_mode_allow: false` makes Envoy reset the decode connection. If the decode pod has already responded, the failure is only recorded. The per-request leg state lives in a per-incarnation object captured by the prefill goroutine before launch, so a late prefill failure can never land on a recycled `RoutingContext` that another request has since taken from the pool (there is a test seam that reproduces the aliasing deterministically). 4. **Observability.** `gateway_pd_prefill_failure_total{class,stage}` (`stage` = `before_response` / `after_response`), `gateway_pd_decode_abort_total{prefill_failure_class,result}`, structured log lines `pd_prefill_fail_fast` and `pd_decode_abort`. The generic request-fail counters carry `status="pd_prefill_failure"` so a fail-fast is separable from an upstream 503. A fail-fast runs `finalizeRouterContext` exactly once and is never counted as a successful request. 5. **Env vars** (documented in `pkg/plugins/gateway/ENV_VARS.md`): `AIBRIX_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (existing), `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_TIMEOUT` (seconds, default 3, `0` disables the abort), `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_RETRY_DELAY` (seconds, default 2, `0` sends a single attempt). 6. **Tests.** Unit tests for the failure classification, the abort scheduling (both attempts, skip-after-response, `0` semantics), the `select` and the fail-fast response, plus a regression test for the pooled-context aliasing. e2e (`test/e2e/gateway/pd/pd_fail_fast_test.go`): `TestPDPrefillFailFastRejectedPrefill` rejects the prefill leg with the mock while holding the decode leg for 10 s (new role-scoped `x-aibrix-mock-delay-role` header on the mock app) and asserts the client is answered with the prefill status + `x-error-pd-prefill: true` before the decode leg could respond, and that a decode mock recorded `/abort_request` with the gateway's rid; `TestPDPrefillFailFastPrefillTimeout` covers the `timeout` class / 503 mapping and skips itself unless the gateway is deployed with a short `AIBRIX_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (exported as `AIBRIX_E2E_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), because the shipped 60 s exceeds the mock's delay cap. The mock app gains an `/abort_request` route so the abort is observable. ### Notes for review - Commits are separable: (1) `LoadEnvNonNegativeInt`, (2) rid + decode abort, (3) client fail-fast, (4) e2e + docs. Each builds and vets on its own. - `http_status` passes the prefill engine's own 4xx/5xx through to the client (502 if it is not a code Envoy names); the other classes map to 503. Happy to switch to "always 503 with the upstream status in the body" if preferred. - `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_TIMEOUT=0` is the off switch for the abort. A dedicated boolean would work as well; this keeps the knob count down. - `TestPDFailureSGLangAsyncPrefillHandoff` now normally sees the gateway's fail-fast response before the decode mock's own 500; its `>= 500` assertion still holds and the decode mock still records its handoff failure. Flagging it in case it flakes on CI. - Race detector is clean on `pkg/plugins/gateway`, `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/pd/...` and `pkg/types`; `make lint` and `make licensecheck` pass. ### Verification on a real deployment Fault injection on a 2-prefill / 2-decode SGLang deployment with a gateway built from the equivalent change, prefill request timeout set to 3 s so that a cold ~24k-token prompt times out on the prefill leg: | scenario | client | decode pod | prefill pod | |---|---|---|---| | prefill timeout, abort enabled | 6/6 got 503 at 3.01 s (before: hang until the engine's 300–600 s bootstrap timeout) | `AbortReq` dequeued + ACKed 6/6, prealloc/transfer queues back to baseline | abort notification in the same second, 6/6 released | | prefill timeout, `AIBRIX_DECODE_ABORT_TIMEOUT=0` | same 503 at 3.01 s | released by the Envoy reset alone ≈1.1 s after the 503 | ≈1.1 s after the 503 | | `kill -9` a prefill pod under load | requests on the dead pod: 503 in 2.2 s (`transport`); requests on the healthy pod: 200 | abort ACKed 4/4 | n/a | No collateral under normal load (≈1,800 requests, ≈65k-token prompts, no injected failures): every abort attempt logged was the "client closed the stream after completion" echo, all after the request's own `request_end` (Δ 0.1–0.6 ms), all skipped because the decode pod had already responded; the engines' `num_aborted_requests_total` did not move on any pod. title: [Bug] Guard ModelGPUProfile.GetSignature against short indexes
body:
## Pull Request Description

`ModelGPUProfile.GetSignature` reads `indexes[i]` once per requested feature but only checks the inner slices, so a profile with fewer index ranges than features (a missing `indexes` field unmarshals to nil) panics with `index out of range`. The gRPC server in `cmd/plugins/main.go` is built without a recovery interceptor, so one malformed profile terminates the plugin process instead of failing a single routing decision.

The Python estimator already treats any dimension mismatch as an error: `get_signature()` raises before doing any work. This adds the equivalent guard on the Go side:

```go
if len(indexes) != len(features) {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("profile index size mismatch, got %d, expected %d", len(indexes), len(features))
}
ret := make([]int, len(features))
```

`rankImpl` propagates `GetSignature` errors and `Peek` logs a warning and skips the profile, so the failure becomes "this deployment was not scored" and the gateway stays up. The guard requires an exact match, so profiles with extra index ranges are rejected as well instead of producing a short signature that fails later in `getValue`.

Verified by reverting the guard locally: the short-index specs fail with `index out of range`, while the extra-index case silently returns a short signature; with the guard, `go test ./pkg/cache/... ./pkg/plugins/gateway/queue/...` passes.

## Related Issues

Related issue: N/A. Found while reading the routing code. I can open one first if that is preferred.

title: [Gateway] Move power-of-two routing onto the shared running-requests counter
body:
## Pull Request Description power-of-two kept its own per-model, per-pod:port counters in Redis (po2_req_count:*), incremented inside Route and decremented through a registered RequestTracker. The cache already maintains a cross-gateway running-request count for every routed request, exposed through Cache.GetPodsRunningRequests, and least-request reads it. Read it from there instead. Route now samples two distinct ready pods, reads both counts in a single GetPodsRunningRequests call, and routes to the lower one. For pods that serve several ports, the port is chosen with the same helper least-request uses. The router keeps no state of its own, so the Redis client, key rotation, tracker hooks and lastRoutingTime are gone, and power-of-two registers via init() like the other routers instead of requiring Redis (RegisterPowerOfTwoRouter and NewPowerOfTwoRouterWithRedis are removed). Without Redis it falls back to this gateway's own counts. Behavior changes: - Counts are per pod, not per model, and include traffic from every router, not only power-of-two. - Counts are shared across gateway replicas, with crashed gateways excluded by the existing liveness window. - The increment now happens when the gateway registers the request, right after Route, rather than inside Route. - Existing po2_req_count:* keys are no longer written and expire on their own. The per-port metric the cache exposes holds the pod's total running count rather than a per-port count, so port choice for data-parallel pods is only approximately load-aware, as it already is for least-request. Tests: the Redis-key tests are replaced with tests that run Route against a fake cache and against a real cache.Store with the gateway's AddRequestCount/DoneRequestCount calls around it. The routing e2e suite gains power-of-two tests for strategy registration, avoiding a pod that another gateway reports as busy, and counters draining back to zero for plain, streamed and concurrent requests. ## Related Issues Resolves: #[Insert issue number(s)] **Important: Before submitting, please complete the description above and review the checklist below.** ---

title: [Bug] Skip profile cache updates when Redis client is nil in standalo…
body:
The gateway-plugin panics with a nil pointer dereference **~10 seconds after startup** in standalone mode without Redis, which contradicts the documented behavior
  (`deployment/local/README.md`: *"Redis is not required in local mode. Without Redis, rate limiting is disabled but routing works normally."*).

  **Panic:**

  ```
  panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

  goroutine 114 [running]:
  github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/cache.(*Store).updateDeploymentProfiles(...)
      pkg/cache/cache_profile.go:36
  github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/cache.initProfileCache.func1()
      pkg/cache/cache_init.go:553
  created by github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg.cache.initProfileCache in goroutine 1
      pkg/cache/cache_init.go:548
  ```

  **Root cause:** `initProfileCache` unconditionally starts the 10s profile-refresh ticker, and on the first tick `updateDeploymentProfiles` calls `c.redisClient.Scan(...)` at
  `pkg/cache/cache_profile.go:36` without a nil check. In standalone mode with no Redis, `main()` deliberately continues with a nil `RedisClient` (warning: *"Running without
  Redis: rate limiting and user auth disabled"*), and `InitOptions.RedisClient` is documented as "Can be nil" — every sibling initializer in `cache_init.go` guards with `if
  opts.RedisClient != nil` (lines 420/425/432) except this one. Regression introduced in #1192 (`cf64e51b`).

  **Fix:** Skip the background refresh loop in `initProfileCache` when `store.redisClient` is nil, logging a warning. Two deliberate choices:

  1. `store.pendingLoadProvider = newPendingLoadProvider(store)` stays **unconditional** — it is consumed by the request-tracing path (`cache_trace.go:355`) independently of
  Redis and must not be disabled by this fix.
  2. The guard is placed inside `initProfileCache` (not at the call site) so the semantics of `enableProfileCaching` ("is the profile feature wanted") remain decoupled from
  Redis availability. Consumers already degrade gracefully when profiles are absent: `GetModelProfileByPod` returns `MissingProfileError`, and `cache_trace.go:372` explicitly
  treats it as non-fatal.

  **Workaround (verified on unpatched binary):** setting `AIBRIX_MODEL_GPU_PROFILE_CACHING_FLAG=false` also avoids the panic, confirming the profile-refresh path is the only
  crash source.

  **Testing:**

  - `go build ./pkg/cache/` and `go vet ./pkg/cache/` pass; `go test ./pkg/cache/` passes.
  - End-to-end on macOS (built `gateway-plugins` with `-tags "nozmq"` from `main` @ `abb2cd20`): standalone mode + `--endpoints-config` + **no Redis running** → unpatched binary
   crashes after the first 10s tick; patched binary stays alive and logs `"Redis client is nil, skipping deployment profile cache updates"` (observed process alive >13s).

  **Open question for maintainers (out of scope here):** in Kubernetes mode, a misconfigured Redis now silently disables profile-based features. A fail-fast at startup (similar
  to `EnableKVSync`'s `klog.Fatalf` at `cache_init.go:439`) could make such misconfiguration visible, but that changes existing behavior and likely deserves its own discussion.

  ## Related Issues

  Resolves: #2754

title: [API] Reject StormService /scale above 1 in Pooled mode
body:
## Pull Request Description

#2450 and #2617 added optional `StormServiceSpec.Mode` and consume it in the controller and PodAutoscaler. Create/update admission already rejects a declared `mode: Pooled` with `spec.replicas > 1`.

That check does not run for the `/scale` subresource. `kubectl scale`, HPA, and other external autoscalers write `spec.replicas` through `/scale`, so a pooled StormService could still be scaled above one RoleSet.

This change registers a validating webhook for `stormservices/scale`. The handler loads the parent StormService, applies the proposed replica count, and reuses `validateStormServiceMode`:

- Declared `mode: Pooled` cannot set replicas > 1 via `/scale`. The admission error tells operators to scale roles through `spec.template.spec.roles[].replicas` instead.
- Declared `mode: Replica` can still scale `spec.replicas`.
- Omitted `spec.mode` is not pinned to inferred Pooled, so existing replica scaling continues to work.

Helm and kubebuilder webhook manifests include the new `vstormservicescale.kb.io` rule.

### Tests

- Unit: reject/allow table for `/scale` (Pooled > 1, Pooled == 1, Replica > 1, omitted mode > 1), plus malformed Scale and missing StormService.
- Integration: envtest `/scale` subresource reject for declared Pooled, allow for declared Replica, allow when mode is omitted.

Verified locally:

```
go test -count=1 ./pkg/webhook/
ok  	github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/pkg/webhook	0.089s

make test-integration-webhook
Ran 84 of 84 Specs in 7.265 seconds
SUCCESS! -- 84 Passed | 0 Failed
```

## Related Issues
Part of #2449. This is the leftover `/scale` subresource enforcement from the follow-up list after #2450 and #2617. It does not close #2449; the original issue still has remaining items such as reporting the resolved mode in status.

title: feat: add Valkey as OSS metadata store option with external managed endpoint support
body:
## Pull Request Description

Adds [Valkey](https://valkey.io/) (Linux Foundation, BSD-3 licensed) as an OSS-licensed
alternative to Redis for the AIBrix metadata store, and wires the existing
`ExternalConnectionConfig` API so operators can point the KV-cache controller at a managed
Valkey/Redis-compatible endpoint (e.g., Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey) instead of an
in-cluster pod.

All changes are purely additive and backward-compatible. Existing Redis configuration is
untouched and remains the default.

### Why

Redis 7.x ships under RSALv2/SSPLv1 (not OSI-approved). Valkey is a wire-compatible fork
under BSD-3. The existing `go-redis` client and all `REDIS_*` env vars work unchanged over
the RESP protocol. This unblocks deployments where open-source license compliance is required.

The `ExternalConnectionConfig` struct already existed in the CRD API — this PR wires it into
the reconcile loop so it is actually functional.

### Changes

**Part 1 — Valkey as a drop-in image option**

- `config/metadata/valkey.yaml` — New K8s Deployment + Service using `valkey/valkey:8-alpine`.
  Service name is `redis-master` so all `REDIS_HOST` references work with no modification.
  Mutually exclusive with `redis.yaml`.
- `deployment/standalone/docker-compose.yml` — Redis image made configurable via `REDIS_IMAGE`
  env var (defaults to `redis:7.4-alpine`). Added `REDIS_SERVER_CMD` / `REDIS_CLI_CMD` for
  healthcheck compatibility with Valkey.
- `hack/release/sync-dependency-images.sh` — Added `valkey/valkey:8` to the release image
  mirror list.
- `deployment/standalone/README.md` — Documented Valkey as an available OSS alternative with
  usage examples.

**Part 2 — ExternalConnectionConfig wiring**

- `pkg/controller/kvcache/backends/distributed.go`:
  - `reconcileRedisService()` now checks `ExternalConnection` first — if set, skips in-cluster
    Redis deployment entirely and cleans up any existing in-cluster Pod/Service during migration
  - Added `validateExternalConnection()` — validates `host:port` format and verifies
    `PasswordSecretRef` secret/key exist (without reading the value)
  - Extracted `parseSecretRef()` and `buildRedisWatcherEnvVars()` — sets `REDIS_ADDR` and
    `REDIS_PASSWORD` via `SecretKeyRef` for both `hpkv` and `infinistore` watchers
  - Added nil-guard for `Runtime` field to prevent panic when only `ExternalConnection` is
    configured
  - Renamed `etcdService` to `metadataService`
- `pkg/controller/kvcache/backends/distributed_test.go` — 5 new subtests covering all
  reconcile paths

### Usage

**Kubernetes — external managed endpoint:**

```yaml
apiVersion: orchestration.aibrix.ai/v1alpha1
kind: KVCache
spec:
  metadata:
    redis:
      externalConnection:
        address: "valkey.example.com:6379"
        passwordSecretRef: "valkey-credentials/password"
```

**Kubernetes — Valkey in-cluster** (swap `redis.yaml` for `valkey.yaml` in kustomization.yaml):

```bash
kubectl apply -f config/metadata/valkey.yaml
```

**Docker Compose — Valkey:**

```bash
REDIS_IMAGE=valkey/valkey:8-alpine \
REDIS_SERVER_CMD=valkey-server \
REDIS_CLI_CMD=valkey-cli \
docker compose up -d
```

### Testing

- Part 1: existing integration tests pass (no behavior change to default Redis path)
- Part 2: 5 new unit subtests — skip in-cluster deployment when external connection is set,
  invalid address format, missing password secret, nil Runtime guard, custom secret key format

## Related Issues

Resolves: 

- Wire compatibility confirmed: https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/issues/928
